I think your biggest issues with Bernie are economic and I presume you're ideologically in favor of laissez-faire economics (please correct me if I'm mistaken), so I'll focus on defending his economic perspective:

If you had an actually free market you would gradually see consolidation across industries due to economies of scale and scope. As time goes on the biggest corporations in each industry would take advantage of the increases in efficiency that economies of scale and scope imply, at which point they'd begin shaping the market to their benefit by abandoning laissez-faire economics for a regulated (or at least coercive) economic environment designed to benefit primarily themselves.

This isn't just hypothetical: it's literally what happened with the robber barons of the late 19th century, leading to the power structure that was revealed by the Pujo Committee (i.e.; JP Morgan and the interlocking directorate, which still exists to this day and can be seen by cross-referencing executives and major investors at Fortune 500 companies with the members of the CFR, the Bilderberg Group, and a handful of think tanks).

Going just a little deeper into analyzing the history of the US economy, it is exactly the deregulated economic environment of the late 1800s that allowed the previously unprecedented (at least in terms of US history) concentration of wealth and power centered around JP Morgan and the Rockefeller family.

The great irony here is that the lax regulatory environment traditionally proposed by libertarians is exactly what led to the absurd concentration of wealth that allowed the big bankers--who, with their wealth, also wielded tremendous political power--to create libertarians' most detested institution, the Federal Reserve:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Federal_Reserve_System#The_National_Monetary_Commission

One last economic subject I want to talk about is taxes. You may think that the tax rates are too high on the rich, but the fact is that the tax rate (and more importantly, the effective tax rate) is lower now than it ever was when the US was at its peak as an economic powerhouse--the effective tax rate on the richest 1% has fallen from 37% in 1979 to under 20%. This has led directly to the increased concentration of wealth that we've seen since 1980 and, as a result, the increased concentration of political power that itself is used to create more wealth for the richest Americans.

TL;DR: I think it's important to recognize that if you're arguing against taxes and for a generally laissez-faire economic regime, then you're promoting neofeudalism (even if it's unintentional). This is an inescapable reality given that the return on capital is greater than the return on labor and given that economic power can be converted into political power which, in turn, can be used to create a regulatory environment that benefits those who already possess economic power.
